name: Commelina Blue
lede: Commelina blue is a dye made from the dayflower, a small blue wildflower, and it was used in Japanese woodblock prints.

sections.title: A blue from a wildflower
sections.body:
The Pigment Compendium says the dayflower, *Commelina communis*, can yield a blue dye [1]. Schweppe (1992) gives its main coloring matter as a metal complex called commelinin, together with flavocommelin, swertisin, awobanin and flavocommelitin [1]. The compendium's table of dye plants notes that Shimoyama and colleagues (1995) found it in ukiyo-e prints, the Japanese woodblock prints [2].

The swatch is a clear mid blue, lighter than [[navy]] and nearer [[royal-blue]] and [[cobalt-blue]]. Dayflower blue is a plant dye, not a mineral pigment, and the compendium lists it alongside other dye plants.

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: This swatch appears in 42 of 23,781 paintings, 0.18 per cent [3]. It peaks in the 1900s, in 8 of 1,674 paintings, 2.8 times the museums' baseline [3]. Inside a painting it usually plays an accent, in 71 per cent of the 28 paintings where it is measured [3]. These are photographs of paintings, not of dyed paper.
